title: Detection of Employee Names
summary: This detection strategy covers collection of employee names and job roles, which an attacker uses to build a target list and to make a message look personal. Names are freely available on team pages, conference agendas, professional social networks and mail directory lookups, so the useful signal is not publication but bulk retrieval. The telemetry that makes it visible is directory or address book query logging, mail platform audit records for global address list searches, web access logs against staff pages and deception accounts that should never receive mail. It fails in practice because recruitment, sales and human resources genuinely perform large directory reads every day.

beginner.definition: An employee name on its own is public and harmless. A list of names with job titles is far more useful to an attacker. The attacker can write to the right person and mention the right project. This detection looks for bulk collection of names rather than for a single public page.
beginner.whyItMatters: A message that uses your name and your manager name feels safe. That is why attackers collect names first. Most organisations publish team pages because they help customers and hiring. Removing all of that information would damage the business. The defence is therefore to notice the collection step. A single account that reads the whole staff directory in one minute is a strong signal. It often arrives days before the phishing campaign.
howItWorks: Your mail server or directory service writes a record each time an account searches for a user.
The detection reads those records and counts how many different users one account looked up.
It compares that count with the normal pattern for the role, such as help desk or recruitment.
It also watches staff pages on your public site for rapid sequential reading.
Deception accounts are checked too, because mail to a name that does not exist shows a harvested list.
When a limit is passed, the rule raises an alert with the account, the count and the time window.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel reception desk with a guest list. Staff may look up one name to connect a call, and that is normal. Now imagine that somebody photographs the entire list in one minute. The list itself is not secret to the staff, but the way it was read is the problem. The receptionist notes the time, the person and the reason given. Your detection is that note. It does not stop the reading, but it tells security that a full list of names has left the building.
takeaways: Names are public, but bulk name collection is a clear warning sign.
Compare directory reads with what the role normally needs to do.
Deception entries catch a harvested address list before the phishing starts.

objectives: Explain how employee names support targeted social engineering.
Identify which logs record directory and address book searches.
Set a query threshold based on the normal pattern for each role.
Design a deception account that reveals a harvested address list.
Describe how to respond when bulk name collection is confirmed.
dataSources: Directory service or lightweight directory access protocol query logs with bind account, search filter and result count
Mail platform audit records for address book and global address list searches per mailbox
Web server access logs for team, leadership and staff directory pages on the public site
Deception mailbox or canary account alerts when mail arrives at an address that no person owns
Inbound mail gateway logs showing a single campaign addressed to many named employees
logic: The pattern is bulk retrieval of employee identity data by a single account or source, followed or preceded by use of that data in targeted mail. The fields that must be correlated are the querying account, the directory filter that was used, the number of distinct user objects returned, the time window and, on the mail side, whether the recipient addresses match the retrieved set. Benign bulk reads come from help desk tools, human resources systems and identity synchronisation jobs that run on a schedule from a service account. The malicious case is a normal user account reading far more objects than its role needs, at an unusual hour, with a filter that selects names and job titles.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Bulk Directory Object Read by a Single User Account
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     protocol: 'ldap'
#     operation: 'search'
#     search_filter|contains: 'objectClass=user'
#   filter_service_accounts:
#     account_name|endswith: '$'
#   filter_sync_jobs:
#     account_name|in: 'identity_sync_accounts'
#   condition: selection and not filter_service_accounts and not filter_sync_jobs | count(distinct object_dn) by account_name > 300
# level: low
falsePositives: Human resources and recruitment staff who search the directory for many candidates in one session.
Identity synchronisation jobs and directory migration tools run by the platform team.
Help desk agents who resolve a batch of mailbox or distribution list requests together.
An automated reporting tool that builds the monthly staff list from the directory.
tuningNotes: First baseline directory read volume per role for two weeks, because help desk and recruitment legitimately exceed a simple count. Add a filter for service accounts and for the identity synchronisation hosts that run on a schedule. Scope the rule to interactive user accounts outside those groups. If you narrow the rule too far you lose the slow collector who reads fifty names each day for a week, so keep a second branch that alerts on a new source address appearing in directory logs for several days in a row.
